articles.title: Slog AM: Trump Declares Oman and Iran’s Strait of Hormuz is Ours, Mariners Humiliated Before Tens of Thousands, Washington Judge Rules Life, Liberty, and Pursuit of Happiness Now Apply to Data Center Power Lines
articles.author: Charles Mudede and Vivian McCall
paras: Conservative KIRO News Radio is now concerned about a report by Washington Health Benefit Exchange that “showed 66,000 people in Washington dropped their Affordable Care Act (ACA).” That’s close to a 25% drop. Since Trump took office, around 100,000 people in this state lost their protection from the accidents of life; they can’t afford to go to the hospital if something suddenly happens, and something bad always happens to the body sooner or later to a body, otherwise it wouldn’t be a bloody body. This is a moral catastrophe of the first order. Conservatives, who often claim to be the followers of “the man from Galilee,” are entirely responsible for this. And, of course, it’s “the meek” who must suffer because of these “thoughts and prayers” white Christians. No one else is to blame. Forty-two percent of those who lost coverage were “under 34, with black and Hispanic residents” bearing the brunt of white American Christianity.

Praise Father God, Amtrak Cascades will resume its service to Portland, the busiest part of its line in the Pacific Northwest , after a fire on August 2 threatened to collapse a warehouse onto the tracks near Union Station. The Seattle Times reports that trains will resume partial service today to Portland; the next day, all trains will carry the people to the great dives and strip clubs of Portlandia. Many of us feared it would take forever to revive the life of this crucial part of the line. But Lord, you showed us your mercy. Praise by thy name.
Trump has declared , on Truth Social , that the Strait of Hormuz is now “ NEW U.S. Territory. ”

What to make of this declaration of madness? It recalls the final scene of Werner Herzog’s Aguirre , the Wrath of God. But that conquistador, Gonzalo Pizarro (played with insane intensity by Klaus Kinski), wasn’t nearly as nuts as Trump at this point. Some of Pizarro’s declarations on the doomed ship, attacked by monkeys and indigenous arrows, proved to be correct. There is no such hope to expect from Trump’s drifting ship.

What Americans have to realize is the American Empire is now a thing of the past. If the US is lucky, it will continue as a tri-polar world: China, Europe, and North America. The last will require the US to open its borders to Canada and Mexico and create, possibly in Washington, D.C., a kind of Brussels . So sorry to say this, but American Awesome is now receding in the rearview mirror. Get used to it.

Recall that excellent line by the British R&B trio Loose Ends: “ It’s all a mystery to me .” The Seattle Times columnist Danny Westneat is somehow saying something similar about a river in Spokane that’s not “ rivering ”: “…for now [it’s] a mystery [to me].” On August 9, a mile of Spokane River went dry just like that. The same thing happened last year, and no one, not even scientists, has any idea why? Can I provide a clue, pretty please? In 2024 , the GOP candidates were all about that cheap gas; this time around, it’s the Democrats. No one in mainstream politics is saying no to gas. It’s only about its cost, which, in terms of social costs (the harm it does to the environment and humans), is way too cheap. If we wanted our dying rivers to rise and live again, we should be paying around $20 for a gallon. (By the way, the Spokesman-Review is not in the dark about what’s what . The Spokane River is dying because of climate change caused by capitalism. What is Westneat on?)

Speaking of rivers dying in the capitalocene (we must not call it the anthropocene because it blames humans in general and not a historically specific culture of humans, one that has as its substance the unlimited accumulation of value—and I use the word “substance” to mean that which is necessary for a certain thing to be a thing—for this climate catastrophe). Anyway, there appears to be no rain coming our way today. Expect a high of 79 today.

Creamed in Milwaukee: If Nathalie were here, and not on vacation at some reservoir, she would despair over the Mariners’ blowout loss to the Brewers 22-0 at American Family Field in Milwaukee. Never in franchise history have the M’s gotten their plump, juicy, brand-sponsored asses kicked this bad. According to the Seattle Times , 36,870 cheerful fans watched this torture scene, which began with the grim portent of a tornado warning.

Guys, the Mariners, I don’t know if you are reading this, but I know losing sucks. But losing really, really catastrophically bad— tying the MLB record for getting pantsed and stuffed into the proverbial locker , joining the Chicago Cubs and Cleveland Guardians New York Yankees*—is something else entirely. It is very funny. As your good friend and starting pitcher Bryce Miller said, y’all still have a chance at the Series. I have only this to say…

Since we’re talking disasters, the professional nerds at the Washington Department of Emergency Management, Department of Natural Resources, and others, modeled an Alaskan tsunami caused by a 9.2 quake along the Alaskan-Aluetian subduction zone—a much more likely scenario than the Big One—and found that a wall of water would indeed slam into our coastline, inundating our islands and charming beach towns with ferocious speed. What they didn’t expect to see were significant impacts on the inner coast of Puget Sound. At least folks would have more time to scramble up the hills in the event of an Alaskan quake than when the Cascadian subduction zone decides to do the tantarella. If you live in the drowning part of the state instead of the burning part of the state, experts urge you to find out how to receive emergency alerts . Also, get yourself a NOAA radio , which can be programmed to alert you to a tsunami’s presence.

Classes at California high school Wheatland Union were canceled yesterday after a bomb threat made by an AI-generated voice. “[This is] consistent with a pattern of hoax threats targeting schools across the country,” reports FOX40. Automated robo bomb threats have shut down schools in Georgia , in Vermont , and in Kansas .
UPDATE: Classes at Wheatland Union were delayed today after a second threat .
WIRED reconstructed Flock camera’s next-generation AI system for monitoring the Shiny Happy People of America and confirmed it does more than track license plates*.

“The software, originally called Nightshift and more recently renamed OS Investigate, ships with 69 prewritten prompts that officers can select, review, or edit, and then submit to the AI. Officers can also input prompts of their own.

The suggested prompts sit in a cache of more than 450 files that WIRED found on Flock’s own website, served by its login pages to anyone who loaded them. The code describes 45 tools at the AI’s disposal, giving it access to plate scans and camera metadata, arrest records, case files, dispatch logs, ballistics results, and commercial databases that contain Social Security numbers, dates of birth, phone numbers, email addresses, relatives and associates.”
*Freudian slip: Google Docs, which includes an annoying predictive text feature, autocompleted this sentence as “confirmed it does more harm than good.” Broken clocks.

Meanwhile, a Washington judge did her part for this technological revolution when she ruled that the Grant County Public Utility District can take land for data center power lines. Grant County Superior Court Judge Jennifer Richardson did not decide whether the utility had followed the “required negotiation and appraisal procedures,” reports the Times , but said it didn’t matter or invalidate the county’s decision to condemn nine properties in the way of the power lines. Unless the parties wave a jury, jurors will decide how much landowners will be paid. One plaintiff claims that Grant PUD valued her property $600,000 less than it was worth.

Frank Beard, the drummer of ZZ Top, and ironically, the trio’s only relatively clean-shaven member, joined the 77 club yesterday . Beard was in hospice care when he died at his ranch in Richland, Texas, not too far from the waterpark where I spent two blazing summers lifeguarding in high school. ZZ Top singer/guitarist Billy Gibbons said in a statement that he lost a true collaborator, and Texas lost a true son. A solemn yee haw.
To reflect, here’s Charles’s favorite ZZ tune: “Blue Jeans Blues.”

*Correction: Justin, a loyal reader and former Ohioan, let me know that, although he understands the concept of Cleveland as America’s punching bag, the Guardians beat the New York Yankees 22-0, not the other way around. “For what it’s worth, Cleveland beat the Yankees 22-0 in 2004, and it is that team from New York that shares the title with the Mariners for worst loss in baseball history. The Yankees already have the most championships and all the money, let’s at least recall their flaws accurately too.” Right you are, Justin. Thanks for your eagle, err, buckeye.

articles.title: UW Tacoma Aspires to Double Enrollment, Become Downtown's Largest Park
articles.author: Carolyn Bick
paras: It wasn’t long into her tenure before Sheila Edwards Lange, the University of Washington-Tacoma’s new chancellor, noticed something puzzling: private companies were buying buildings in what appeared to otherwise be the university’s campus footprint.
“I thought we owned all of that property, and so when I saw new highrises going up, I thought, ‘Well, how is that possible?’” Lange said.

At the time, developers were also advocating for zoning changes in the campus’ footprint. There was no way the campus could grow to realize any of the aspirations laid out in its old campus master plan , she said, “because our old campus master plan also called for us to be 10,000 students once we were fully built out. […] I was very alarmed — not that folks were doing what they do, which is building housing, which we need, but that the future of the campus was really at risk.”

Lange became the university’s chancellor in 2021. In addition to handling university operations and strategy during the early stages of the Covid pandemic, she had also inherited the legacy of a particular kind of expansion strategy the university had employed since it first opened its doors more than 35 years ago. Instead of having a traditional campus, the university has historically bought up empty buildings — many of them leftover from Tacoma’s industrial past — in the surrounding area, and converted them into classrooms. The 22 buildings the campus now owns are spread over 46 acres.

Now, that’s all changing. Complete with new buildings, the university is pursuing a central campus design meant to (literally) center student life and further its stated goal of reaching 10,000 full-time undergraduate and graduate students.

But a design focused on student life doesn’t necessitate siloing the students from the wider community. Instead, the design intentionally keeps specific corridors and sightlines open and introduces significantly more greenspace to foster community connection and connection with nature. It also preserves significant older buildings on campus, alongside creating new ones to expand student living and dining options.

When UW Tacoma opened in 1990, it didn’t have a dedicated campus in the traditional sense. Conceptualized as an option for transfer and graduate students, the university aimed to serve a South Sound population for whom leaving the area, let alone the state, was not an option.

At the time, there were several otherwise empty buildings connected with the city’s past as the western terminus for the Northern Pacific Railroad. The university was originally housed in one building, the historic Perkins building, which the university leased and did not own. The university could only accommodate 187 students and only offered one degree: liberal studies.

But that swiftly changed. In 1997, the university moved office operations to its current, permanent location on Pacific Avenue, and continued to grow and expand, taking up classroom residence in otherwise empty buildings.

The university now serves about 5,000 students and operates in several converted warehouses and historic buildings in the area. Of the university’s 22 buildings, 18 are historic. Roughly half of the university’s students matriculate directly from high school, while the other half enroll later in life. Many utilize the multiple modes of transit readily available to get to the university.

Over the years, as the university bought up empty buildings for university, a distinct campus footprint emerged. That footprint holds several older buildings, including culturally significant gathering places, and even a tree that is more than a century old.

Following Lange’s observation about the private companies buying up buildings within the campus footprint, the university put out a request for proposals. Given that the university could only afford to pay $350,000 for design work, they didn’t think they would get many bidders, Joe Lawless, the university’s chief strategy officer, said — but “we got 18 [bids].”

That the Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) was one of those bidders came as even more of a shock, Lawless said, after the university chose to partner with the firm. BIG is a 20-year-old, international architecture and design firm that places ecology, natural connection and sustainability at the center of its work. Its team has won dozens of awards for architecture and design, and has held exhibitions around the world.

Yu Inamoto, a BIG associate and one of the campus design team members, said in an email that BIG threw its hat in the ring to design the campus because the firm saw the sheer potential for the area and the campus.

Neither the university nor BIG worked in a vacuum. Lawless said that BIG “did a really good job” of engaging not just students and faculty, but community members in the process. He estimated that about 80 community groups gave feedback on the project.

The design that emerged was one that prioritizes green space and a space for both students and the wider Tacoma community to thrive. The design intentionally places the central commons area next to the new campus dorms, and specifically creates sightlines to the waters of Puget Sound, and to Tahoma, also known as Mount Rainier.

“The day before they published the final version of the plan [… Inamoto] called me and said, ‘I need you to go up to that corner and stand precisely at the corner and take a picture of the mountain because we need to make sure the access is perfectly aligned from that corner to the peak of the mountain,’” Lawless said.
Right now, where the university sits shows up as a bright red splotch on heat maps, Lawless said, but he refers to the future campus as “Tacoma’s largest park.”

After speaking with residents, Lawless realized just how important it is to make the space into a center not just for academia, but for the wider public. Several residents he spoke with were elders, he said, and they told him that the areas around the current campus footprint are where they spend the most time — “your campus is our park. Your campus is where we go to have our trees and open space. […] It's where people are and you feel safer.”
Inamoto said that in designing the UW Tacoma campus master plan, the company wanted to weave public and greenspace together into the university environment.

“By proposing a cascading urban landscape that brings together these open spaces, we can better connect the campus internally while also integrating it more naturally within Tacoma,” he explained. “This way, students can feel more ingrained in both the campus community and the broader neighborhood.”

In addition to the green-centric layout, Inamoto said that BIG suggested the university work with one of Tacoma’s native tree programs, Grit City Trees , and plant trees along sidewalks and open space.

Despite data showing nationwide college enrollment steadily dropping over the last decade and projected to continue that same downward trend, UW Tacoma aims to double student enrollment from 5,000 students to 10,000 students.

New student housing and dining options will play a role in making going to school at UW Tacoma more affordable and attractive for students. The university plans to create both a more traditional residence hall that will have between 400-500 beds and a dining hall. Lange said that the university expects to open the residence hall in 2029.

The university has an apartment building where mostly older students and graduate students live. While that building has two apartments set aside for emergency housing for housing-unstable students, there are no other university living options for students. UW Tacoma also does not have a dining hall.

According to the university’s most recent survey , 55% of UW Tacoma’s students are food insecure, while 36% are housing insecure. These are higher than normal percentages, Lange said, and having the option of a residence hall and a dining hall will help relieve some of this burden.

“Having a traditional residence hall means they don't have to have credit checks in order to get housing,” Lange explained. “They can get nine months or 12 months, if that's what they want, but they don't have to sign a year-long agreement the way they would in a commercial housing development.”

The university hasn’t yet determined the cost to live in the planned residence hall or have a meal plan, but the university’s director of communications, Elizabeth Metcalf, said in an email that the goal is to make living and dining more accessible for students.

“As we develop these offerings, affordability, flexibility and access will remain key priorities,” Metcalf said. “Because food costs can fluctuate and we are still in the early stages of negotiations with a food service provider, meal plan pricing will not be available until closer to the dining hall's anticipated opening in autumn 2029.”

Mentha Hynes-Wilson, vice chancellor of student life, said that centering students is one of the university’s goals in the new campus design, which the university is hoping will entice more students to enroll. Deciding to enroll in a school is not just about academics, she said. It’s also about whether a student can see themselves succeeding, staying, and belonging in a community.

“The residence and dining hall are designed to feel welcoming, connected, and full of energy. Open spaces will flow into more intimate gathering areas, creating opportunities to meet friends, study, collaborate, and build community. Flexible spaces, courtyards, a kitchenette, and quieter areas will support everything from events and music practice to studying and recharging,” Hynes-Wilson said in an email. “We’re also excited to expand living-learning communities, connecting where students live with how they learn. Students can study together, participate in shared activities, build friendships, and develop relationships with peers, faculty, and staff that make residence life an extension of the educational experience.”
“Ultimately,” she continued, “we want prospective students to walk onto this campus and think, ‘This is where I belong. This is where I want to build my future.’”

Lange said that the university hasn’t set a specific date for the 10,000-student enrollment target — she sees it happening over the next 30 years — but there are specific dates that the university plans to complete key buildings. Provided the university gets capital funding from the state, the university will complete renovations of its historic buildings by 2030, and projects that the park portion of the campus will be completed in the autumn of 2031.

Like most United States institutions, the university sits on land whose history is fraught with colonization and racism. Tacoma’s history includes the forced removal of Indigenous people , anti-Chinese riots , the incarceration of Japanese Americans , and the continuing legacy of redlining . It is this history that the university has long worked to address, including in the new campus’ design.
In addition to meeting with city leaders, Lange said, the university has also made a point of regularly meeting with and incorporating feedback from the Puyallup Tribe.

“What we've heard from them is that they really feel like we are listening to them and incorporating everything that they are advising us to do into the plan, like story poles and art and the desire to one day have a longhouse here on campus,” Lange said.

At its northernmost edge along Tacoma Avenue, the university borders on the Hilltop neighborhood. The Hilltop is an historically Black neighborhood that evolved from redlining and racist lending practices. The community has recently faced increased displacement pressure, as Tacoma has become a regionwide destination for people escaping higher rents elsewhere, which has in turn led to rents jumping in Tacoma. Expanded services, such as the Hilltop extension of the Tacoma streetcar , have boosted interest from developers and real estate investors. The combination has driven up property values beyond what many generational residents can afford.
The university said it has made a point of prioritizing the Hilltop community’s concerns, needs, and wants.
“We were very conscious of not wanting to contribute to further gentrification of the Hilltop,” Lange said.

“And one of the things that was most surprising and disturbing for me was that people really felt like […] the campus had really turned its back on the Hilltop in some ways, because that part of our campus is really unkempt. It is overgrown and it just doesn't look very welcoming or inviting.”

articles.title: Mildred’s Death Day
articles.author: Evanne Hall, Charles Mudede, Amanda Manitach, and Emily Nokes
paras: On December 9, 2019, my grandma—wearing her favorite dress, with her hair set and makeup applied—sat in her favorite recliner, surrounded by family at home, and raised a glass of strawberry daiquiri for a toast. We all yelled “kanpai!” She thanked us, and drank. Eighteen minutes later, she was dead.

Mildred was a complicated woman to love. She was not a hugger or giver of compliments. While she was exceptionally generous (money was her preferred gift to give), had a good sense of humor, and was adored by her friends and neighbors, everything needed to be on her terms. People came to her, she did not go to them.

She had always been pragmatic regarding death, so it was no surprise when, on her 98th birthday, she told my mom and aunt that she wanted to look into the Our Care, Our Choice Act Hawai’i had enacted six months earlier. Her health had been declining; mentally she was sharp, but physically her legs and eyes were giving out. She would rather be dead than unable to do laundry and cook. After some brief research, we determined that she met all but one requirement to move forward with the process: being terminally ill.

The next few months were a blur of travel to Honolulu from the mainland. We split our time between getting her affairs in order, and medical scans—trying to find something, anything , to make her eligible. She had already survived colon cancer, and for a brief moment, when a dark spot appeared on a scan, we were all genuinely hoping that grandma had breast cancer. She did not. She was annoyed. Eventually her doctors declared her congestive heart failure as terminal enough , given her age and quality of life after she had fallen in the shower in August. She was elated. She picked her death day.

In November, more than 100 people came to the house for her celebration of life. Friends and family, mostly local, but many from the mainland, lined up to pay their respects and tell her how much they loved her. She took note of who did not show up.

Then her death day arrived. Around 12 p.m. on December 9, her doctor called to say that he was running late but would be there ASAP. Mildred was upset: She was hoping to be dead before 2 p.m. She was more upset when she found out that her three medicine doses needed to be spaced out 30 minutes apart. By the final, lethal dose, she was out of patience and barely waited for my dad to tell her it was the big one before she had finished it. She was ready.

Her doctor noted that it was the most peaceful death he had ever witnessed and we should all be so lucky to go out on our own terms, surrounded by exactly who we wanted. That was Mildred, always in control. I sure do miss her. EVANNE HALL

There is this idea that all death is just death. And all of us are dissolved, in the end, by this oneness: ashes to ashes, dust to dust. We were persons in life; we are all just nothing in the universal nothingness of death. Death is the ultimate democracy: Elon Musk will go the same way as a person living in a tent near what remains of Rainier Mall, which was destroyed by a fire in 2023 and is now an economic graveyard. But this is not at all what happens. A death is not dissolved into the great all-for-one. The death of an individual is as singular as their life.

Recall how a Looney Tunes character, when fleeing Wile E. Coyote or Elmer Fudd, punches a hole through a brick wall in the perfect shape of its body. Death does this to its survivors, but the shape of the dead’s departure doesn’t correspond with the shape of the departed’s body. Instead, it corresponds with something that’s intrinsic to the space they took up in you.
But that doesn’t mean that the shape of their departure can be predetermined.

Because this is hard to explain, I must use my personal experience of loss. All of the members of my first immediate family are dead. My mother, father, sister, brother—gone. I loved them all equally but each entered death unequally.

In a way, this is to be expected. My mother, in life, was not at all like my father. She was practical, and, though a professor, ran a popular bar in the middle of a city (Gaborone, Botswana), a fact that embarrassed my father because he saw himself as a bit of gentleman: read books, drank good whiskey, and philosophized about the nature of humans and the world in general (he was, above all, a theologian). Business was beneath him.
And so it is: A death is as singular as a life.
My mother’s departure left me deeply reflective. The hole she left in me was philosophical: What is death exactly? Do we go anywhere? Will I ever see her again?
My mother did not believe in hell, but my father did. You would think, then, that his death would make me more philosophical than my mother’s.

Instead, his departure was worldly, all business: the accounts he mismanaged, the secrets he hid from me, the clumsiness of it all. And so the hole he left when exiting life turned out to make me more upset, more worked up, than sad. He should have done this, he should have done that, he shouldn’t have been so aloof. The hole he left was frustration, and my frustration with his ghost will go on until I’m gone.

My brother’s death hit me much harder than expected. I thought I was never that close to him (he was 12 years younger than me and died in 2019 at the age of 37). I didn’t like his music or his bands, and I thought he was born lazy. But, my God, his death to me had the drama and power of Jesus Christ being nailed to the cross.

He did not want to die. He wanted more time. And he did not hide, to me and others close to him, his absolute fear of the nothingness that was fast approaching him. He looked at death with horror. And so the hole he left is still raw, still painful to me

My sister’s death, which happened two years ago, I feared would hit me with a force that surpassed that of my brother’s. She was only two years younger than me. I spent the greater part of my life with her. But her death didn’t blow me away. And I now know why.

Though she’s gone—I have no illusions about that—the hole she left was so large, it was unimaginable. I just can’t process the scale of her departure. Indeed, if I were to see her in a bar on Pike or Pine or somewhere in London, the city she lived in before she died, I would not be in the least surprised. CHARLES MUDEDE

Sometimes I think about post-mortem earworms. The thought will randomly cross my mind while I’m driving and I’ll frantically make a note for a playlist for when I’m dying. Crystal Castles. “Summertime Sadness.” “Bittersweet Symphony.” Gentle techno and all the kinds of things I listen to while driving or in the shower. In case we cling to the last things we hear, I want my earworms in the afterlife to be the ones I loved in life. I’m not sure, but I think this is important enough that it should probably go in people’s wills.

Death was never foreign to me: I grew up touching cold, stiff bodies because my father was a Methodist minister who officiated weddings and funerals all the time (and I was a curious kid). I hated weddings because everyone seemed stressed. I loved funerals because there was always cherry pie afterward. There were a lot of funerals in our tiny west Kansas community, where elderly German American congregants dropped like flies about once a month. My mom wasn’t a good cook, so I was always excited to hear that one of the parishioners had passed. We would eat well.

Somewhere between the latticed crust and the open caskets, I learned what death was supposed to mean. I was 5 the day we filed out of a funeral home and I asked my dad. He pointed to a beetle lying upside down on the sidewalk and explained that both the bug and the body we’d just left behind were empty shells. But it was okay, because: heaven.

I don’t believe in heaven anymore, but I do believe in art. As a recovering pastor’s kid, I think a lot about the parallels between art and religion. The role of an art community is not unlike church. Art has the profound ability to transmit otherwise ineffable feelings that hover over the precipice of the sublime. It can invoke altered states, ecstasy, moments of transcendence. But can it help us comprehend death?

A lot of art skirts mortality without quite touching it. Munch’s mourners in lachrymose shades of blue and black tell of grief. Hans Holbein’s grinning plague skeletons are the great equalizer. Egon Schiele’s subjects are imbued with a sensual death rattle—Eros and Thanatos enmeshed, skeletons half-visible beneath the flesh. Arnold Böcklin’s Isle of the Dead looms, ensorcelling, dragging the viewer inward with a terrifying gravitational pull.

In 1960, Yves Klein—creator of the famous eponymous shade of blue—created the photomontage Leap Into the Void (Le Saut dans le Vide) . The iconic black-and-white image shows the artist suspended midair after flinging himself from a second-story ledge. His body is nearly horizontal, frozen above the street. Another figure pedals away on a bicycle, oblivious to the apparent catastrophe unfolding behind him.

Something Klein captures in this image feels correct: I think we’re all a little bit Klein—flying, dying—but also the guy trying to just mind his business and stay upright on the bike, unwilling to look death full in the face.
But there’s only one artwork, for me, that perfectly gets at the paradox of dying: Damien Hirst’s The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living .

It might just be the title that’s doing the heavy lifting. The work itself, a 14-foot tiger shark preserved in a tank of murky emerald formaldehyde, has been famously fraught, in terms of holding together; the flesh of the beast, first interred in its tank in 1991, wasn’t properly preserved, and it eventually fell off the bone. In 2006, the old shark was replaced with a brand new one—this time embalmed.

The work’s physical failure is inseparable from its conceptual success—the material integrity (or lack thereof) functions in tandem with the mental gymnastics put forward by Hirst in the title. As such, I put forth that it’s the most perfect vanitas ever created: An unparalleled vanity that underscores the hubris of an artist trying to fuck with death like that in the first place.
I’ll probably die without ever understanding death, and I’m okay with that. In the meantime, don’t lose my playlist and pass the cherry pie. AMANDA MANITACH

One year ago this month, I said goodbye to my beloved kitty, Vangelis, at the veterinary emergency room in the middle of the night. I am a very “good in crisis” type of person, but after the clinician told me he was gone, I stood alone in the empty waiting room and wailed in a way that felt ancient and uncontrollable.
In the following days and weeks I was numb, and trying very hard to present as a “normal” amount of sad.

After all, I’d had three years to prepare for this—Vangie was diagnosed with congestive heart failure at the age of 1. I became a CHF medication expert, and I doted on him. I tried to memorize his entire being with enough detail I could holographically project him back into my life at a later date. I had not wasted any of our time together. I thought, then, that I could circumvent some of the mourning process. We had already been through so much.

Instead, I was spun into a state of grief that felt disorienting in its magnitude. This grief felt erratic, white-hot, and embarrassing; I blubbered at the wrong times and dissociated at the wrong times. I broke out in hives and my lymph nodes were swollen and angry.

My friends were lovely and caring, but I was acutely aware that any amount of time spent in mourning, beyond a week, felt “prolonged.” This was made all the more surreal because a dear friend/mentor had died just a month earlier. After his passing, though, there was an entire community who missed him terribly—we could check in, gather, talk about it at length; eventually he would have a massive celebration of life where we could begin to integrate this loss.
My kitty only had his little world. Our little world. The thought that only a small handful of people would ever really understand how perfect and extraordinary he was felt like a universal error.
Somewhere in the cremation paperwork, I was handed a brochure called Understanding Loss and What Happens Next .

Brochures? At a time like this? I expected antiseptic language, corporate reassurance. But, because I did not, in fact, “understand loss” and could not imagine “what happens next” I gave it a read. The writing was so simple and so caring it caught me off guard.

“Give yourself grace and embrace your emotions,” it began. “Grief is not an obstacle. It can’t be avoided or outsmarted. The only way to get to the other side is to go through it.” Of course this was information I’d encountered before, but the simple and careful way it had been put together moved me. There was evidence of human attention behind it. Someone—or likely several people—on the other side of this brochure, had sat down and tried to anticipate what a devastated stranger might need to hear upon leaving an emergency veterinary hospital without the animal they brought in.

articles.title: Fall 2026 Service Change: Pierce County and South King County
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Starting August 29, King County Metro, Sound Transit, and Pierce Transit will be making changes to bus routes in south King County and Pierce County. Most of these changes are in response to the Federal Link Link Extension that opened in December 2025. Service changes in east and north King County will be discussed in future articles.

Across this sub-region, the biggest change is Sound Transit’s Route 574. Route 574 will be truncated at Federal Way Downtown station (instead of SeaTac) and will now run every 15 minutes. At the southern end of the route, the stop at Lakewood Transit Center will be replaced by a stop at Lakewood station.

Routes throughout south King and Pierce Counties will be adjusted in a few weeks. See full list of changes below, or skip to Burien and SeaTac , Kent and Des Moines , Auburn and Federal Way , Pierce County , or Night-Owl changes.

Route 121 will be partially restored to provide eight peak hour trips (four AM and four PM) between Burien Transit Center and downtown Seattle. This route will take just 37 minutes compared to 53 minutes on the H Line.

Route 156 will have a slightly revised routing on its trips between Southcenter and Kent Des Moines station. The route will no longer serve the McMicken Heights loop (dashed blue line on the map). The route will also have expanded service, running from 4am to 11pm on weekdays and 4:30am to 11pm on weekends.
DART Route 631 will now have weekend service. The route will operate the same schedule on Saturday and Sunday as it does during the week.

Route 164 is a new route that will replace the southern half of the current Route 165. Route 164 will run every 15 minutes during the day, every day. Some of the route’s northbound trips will continue to Route 166. Route 166 replaces the northern segment of Route 165. Buses will run every 15 minutes during peak hours and every 30 minutes during the rest of the day. Every southbound trip will continue to Route 164.
Route 168 will have a few additional trips added to provide 15 minute frequency during peak hours.
Route 181 will have improved weekday frequency and addition trips that run until midnight.
Route 182 will have earlier and later trips each day and will now be through-routed with Route 187.
Route 183 will add service on Sunday and run earlier and later on weekdays and Saturday.
Route 187 will be adjusted to run on 320th St and Hoyt Rd in both directions. The route will through-run with Route 182.

DART Route 902 is a new route that will replace DART Route 901. Route 902 has a DART service area in Mirror Lake. Every Route 902 trip will continue to/from a Route 903 trip. DART Route 903 offers a southern route via SW Campus Dr back to Federal Way Downtown station. Route 903 will have increased frequency with trips running every 30 minutes.

King County Metro is introducing two new Metro Flex pilot areas in Federal Way and Auburn. The Federal Way area is anchored at Federal Way Downtown station while the Auburn area is set near Auburn station and transit center.

Pierce Transit’s network is relatively stable for this restructure. Route 11 is getting a new northbound trip at 2pm on weekdays and several other trip times have been adjusted to accommodate the new trip. Route 212 will have a new southbound trip on Sundays at 7:08pm. Pierce Transit is also adding a new westbound trip to Route 214 on Sundays at 8:44am. The agency is also adjusting the schedules for an assortment of routes to improve reliability and reduce transfer times. Sound Transit is removing routes 580 and 586 in Pierce County.

South King and Pierce Counties have two big changes in overnight service. The A Line will now run every 30 minutes between midnight and 4am. Sound Transit is replacing Route 570 with Route 597. Route 597 will provide night-owl service every 30 minutes between Lakewood and Seattle, via Tacoma Dome and SeaTac.

articles.title: Pike Place Pedestrian Pilot Poised to Scale Back for Winter
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: In a move that will likely be a tough pill for Seattle urbanists to swallow, the current pedestrian pilot at Pike Place Market is set to get scaled back to three days a week in October, as the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) tries to find an equilibrium that pleases all stakeholders at the Market. SDOT's proposal would only implement "soft closures" of Pike Place between Pike Street and Virginia Street from 11am to 4pm Friday through Sunday, with "hard closures" with full barricades only implemented during special events.

Outside those weekend and event days, at least through March 31, all vehicles would be allowed to use the corridor without restrictions. According to SDOT's proposal, set to be presented to the Pike Place Market Historical Commission next week, new signage will instruct drivers to yield to pedestrians, with many of the barriers added to manage the busy street through the FIFA World Cup removed.

The current pilot program restricts vehicles simply wishing to drive through the street from accessing Pike Place from 10am to 4pm daily, and has been a smashing success by most metrics. Sales data shows increased business and a jump in visitors, especially locals heading to the Market more often. But it hasn't been viewed as a positive change by many inside the Market, including a substantial slice of business owners and Market advocates.

The question of how the pilot would evolve toward a more permanent iteration has remained an open one, with SDOT holding stakeholder meetings throughout the spring and into the summer to come to a consensus. In addition to SDOT staff, those meetings have included the Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA), the Pike Place Merchants' Association, the Historical Commission, and a representative from Mayor Katie Wilson's office.

Next week's presentation notes that a June survey of nearly 5,500 Market visitors found "near universal" support for vehicle barriers at Pike Place, with only 2% not on board. In the survey, 38% of respondents affirmed the idea that there was an increase in pedestrian safety, and 25% cited a more welcoming environment for Market visitors.

But a presentation slide referencing "key learnings from summer operations" asserts that signage updates could "improve clarity to reduce confusion of who may enter and when." If SDOT surveyed visitors on whether they'd like to see the pilot scaled back for winter, the department has not released those findings.

The shift to weekend-only operations through the winter mirrors a recommendation made by the University of Washington's Urban Freight Lab (UFL), which conducted interviews and surveyed both merchants and visitors over the course of this year. But the information relied on to make that recommendation is anecdotal, and does not appear to be based on any data that suggests the benefits of pedestrianization wouldn't continue to be seen through the winter months.

"This recommendation stems from both the merchant interview/survey and analysis of the visitor survey," the UFL's technical memo based on its analysis, released last month, stated. "Merchants reported reductions in sales or reduced growth was particularly acute during the winter holiday season. The typical 'busy season' occurs between May and September when the maximum number of workers are employed for over 70% of merchants. This corresponds to visitor activity: over 70% of reported visits occur between May and September."
In shifting to a scaled-back schedule for winter, the new plan makes a big concession to the idea that the pedestrian pilot is hurting a subset of businesses within the Market.

"The Merchants report relying on local shoppers heavily during winter months," the memo continues. "Visitors who travel to the Market by car are more likely to visit between October and April than visitors by other modes. Allowing access to passenger vehicles during these months would support Market businesses while minimizing conflicts with pedestrians."

During "full closures," the crash-rated Archer barriers that have been in place this summer would be replaced with more easily movable barricades, suggesting the department has moved beyond an initial safety-related justification for those barriers that was cited in the wake of the 2025 truck attack in New Orleans.

Bollards that had been added to the sidewalk at First Avenue and Pike Street would be removed, with retractable bollards in the street an uncertain prospect given that the ground underneath is not actually solid and features an " areaway " of the type found all around downtown.

Just last week, the nonprofit Allied Arts of Seattle – which holds two seats on the Market Historic Commission – held a discussion on the future of street access on Pike Place, which featured Pike Place Public Development Authority (PDA) Chief Operating Officer Katie Trent and SDOT's Radcliffe Dacanay, who is managing the access project.

"The needs of the market are a little bit different in the fall and winter, so we've been asked to think about what are some of our options, and this would be one of them: Monday through Thursday," Dacanay told attendees. "The conversation is constant, and we want to make sure we're also hearing the voices from the constituency, the merchants' association. So that has been all part of the process, and all of that feedback is coming into SDOT to our engineering department. We're not making decisions off on our own. We're constantly in communication with the PDA, asking what works, what doesn't work, how might we adjust, and it can go from details of the signage. Should we say 11 to 4, 10 to 5? What color? All of these things. We're having that conversation."

As the day-to-day operator of the entire Market, having the PDA's buy-in for the pedestrian pilot's next phase will be pretty essential, with Trent making it fairly clear last week that the PDA is on board with the direction that things are trending in. It was under the leadership of PDA President and CEO Rachel Ligtenberg, who was hired in late 2024, that the pilot was able to happen in the first place.

"There are as many opinions on the street as people providing them. Visitors are generally aligned [...] in generally preferring fewer cars on the street. But we know that grocery merchants and their customers skew much more heavily in favor of access to Pike Place to make their grocery shopping trips happen quickly," Trent said. "I think we're in a really great place coming into our next [iteration] with MHC and the proposal for fall and winter."

The panel was moderated by John Turnbull, the PDA's former Director of Asset Management, who provided a defense of allowing vehicle access along the street that echoed previous odes to the prior status quo, like former city councilmember Peter Steinbrueck calling the mixing of traffic modes "zesty" in 2022 . Turnbull now serves on the Honorary Advisory Board for Friends of the Market, a group that has recently been trying to throw cold water on the positive sales data coming out of the Market.
"What I think is lost by any kind of strict regulation of what happens on the street is a sense of theater and surprise and mystery," Turnbull said.
Gordon Padelford, Executive Director of the Seattle Street Alliance, offered a defense of the current iteration of the pilot that SDOT seems poised to shift away from.

"We've got a number of opinions on what constitutes like a delicate ballet. I don't think random cars driving through the middle are part of that ballet. I think they are a hindrance to people's shopping experience," Padelford said. "I think that's why we've heard in some of the feedback that there's real frustration around what does the signage mean, because a lot of visitors are hoping to have that experience being able to walk with their families down the street, being able to push a stroller, push a wheelchair down the street, and not deal with the random vehicles. So I would say, if you're not actively loading and unloading, it's really not a good use of the street."

The Market Historical Commission will be asked to sign onto the pilot's next iteration at its August 26 meeting, with the certificate of approval for the current phase expiring at the end of September.
An earlier version of this story incorrectly attributed a quote from John Turnbull to Ben Frey of Don & Joe's Meats. We regret the error.
Doug Trumm contributed reporting to this story.

articles.title: Sunday Video: High Oil Prices Can Make Better Cities
articles.author: Stephen Fesler
paras: The latest global oil crisis has been precipitated by an Trump's illegal war in Iran, disrupting global oil supply. The war is nearing its sixth-month mark with no end in sight, and as a consequence oil prices are very high. And while that is certainly problematic to the well-being people in the United States and across the global, past oil crises have led to better cities and environmental outcomes, as Jason Slaughter of Not Just Bikes shows in this video.

The 1970s oil crisis nudged the Netherlands to prioritize bike, pedestrian, and transit investments over cars. Likewise, Canada responded by planning and investing transit projects. France adopted widespread use of nuclear energy, which is still in use today. American regulators adopted better fuel efficiency for motorized vehicles. With the latest global oil crisis, how will cities and countries respond now?

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: West Seattle Link Update
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: At the Sound Transit Board System Expansion Committee meeting on Thursday, the agency shared a series of updates on the upcoming West Seattle Link Extension . The grand opening for the 3.9 mile extension from SODO to Alaska Junction has slipped from 2032 to 2035. This delay is due to longer than expected construction time for building the new bridge to West Seattle. Starting in 2035, 3 Line trains will shuttle passengers across the Duwamish Waterway where they will transfer to the 1 Line in SODO. West Seattle passengers will need to wait until the second tunnel is complete in 2042 before they can enjoy a one-seat-ride to downtown Seattle in the first tunnel.

Sound Transit also shared a new $100 million in project savings achieved through a redesign in how key Seattle City Light infrastructure is relocated. Earlier designs required additional construction on 6th Ave for the 230 kilovolt power lines, but the new approach has moved this infrastructure to be located within the light rail corridor. These savings are part of the nearly $2 billion saved by various other design changes to the extension, including the removal of Avalon station.

The System Expansion Committee approved a resolution to start the acquisition process for 55 properties located along the planned right-of-way. This includes 19 homes, industrial facilities, railroads, and City or County owned land. Sound Transit will begin the appraisal process for each property and start negotiations with the current owners within the next year. Tenants usually have 18 months to relocate.

articles.title: An Eater’s Guide to Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: Seattle is nestled in one of the most beautiful regions of North America. On clear days, you can look west over Puget Sound to see the Olympic Mountains and east across Lake Washington to the Cascades. The metro area is home to immigrant communities from all over Asia as well as Mexico, Central America, Ethiopia, and Somalia; there is also a substantial Indigenous population here. The cultural and ethnic diversity, combined with the wide range of local ingredients, makes the area a fertile ground for restaurants.

Owning a restaurant is a financially risky proposition in the best of times, and area owners are struggling with rising costs, especially now that the tipped minimum wage has expired in Seattle . But that hasn’t dampened the creativity of local chefs: 2025 saw a wave of exciting restaurant openings, and noteworthy new spots are always popping up . Here is a guide to the city’s ever-changing dining scene.

Washington is an agriculturally rich state, and Seattle restaurants benefit from an abundance of nearby farms, fruit orchards , fisheries, shellfish farms , ranches, and wineries . But the city is most famous for its seafood. Salmon is such a part of the area’s culinary identity that in the past, Sea-Tac Airport literally rolled out a red carpet for the first Copper River salmon of the season to arrive from Alaska. Shellfish is a Seattle staple, with many places serving oysters plucked out of its surrounding cold, nutrient-rich waterways. One local delicacy-bordering-on-novelty is the humble geoduck (pronounced “gooey duck”), an enormous clam that sometimes catches newcomers off guard because it looks like a penis.

Seattle features many great cuisines but is perhaps known best for its Asian restaurants. The city has an exceptional Japanese food scene and is home to world-class sushi masters — most notably Shiro Kashiba — and sustainable sushi pioneers like Taichi Kitamura. Pho is ubiquitous around town , and teriyaki — that sticky-sweet Japanese American dish — is a Seattle specialty, popularized by Toshihiro Kasahara at Toshi’s Teriyaki Restaurant in the 1970s (Kasahara still makes teriyaki at his latest restaurant, which is up north in Mill Creek). The Chinese restaurant scene is diversifying to include more regional cuisines, such as Sichuan . Bubble tea is also ubiquitous, and you can find some excellent options at old-school spot Seattle Best Tea or the University District location of Taiwanese chain Don’t Yell At Me . (The U District runneth over with bubble tea.)

But perhaps the hottest cuisine in Seattle is Filipino. Filipino immigrants have lived here since the 19th century, and Pike Place institution Oriental Mart is a testament to the longtime influence of Filipino cuisine. However, in the past half-decade, there’s been an explosion of innovative restaurants, like Melissa Miranda’s Musang and Aaron Verzosa and Amber Manuguid’s Archipelago (the latter of which was nominated for a 2025 James Beard Award ). There is also a bevy of buzzy but more casual Filipino-influenced spots, like the Chicken Supply , Moto Pizza , Hood Famous Bake Shop , and Ludi’s Restaurant .
Eater publishes plenty of maps detailing the top places and things to eat and drink in Seattle. Here are a few of our most popular guides to help you get started:

New Restaurants: This list changes every two months and includes restaurants that have opened or reopened in the last six months. Right now, notable new spots include the biang biang noodle champion Lily Wu’s waterfront seafood boil spot, Happy Crab ; Pioneer Square pastry shop and summer soft-serve stop the Pastry Project ; and new-wave Italian American restaurant Uncle Dom’s Italian Kitchen .

Essential Restaurants: If you need to narrow down the quarterly guide to Seattle’s 38 standout dining destinations even further, you might start at Off Alley , a 14-seat restaurant in a renovated brick alleyway in Columbia City, with its hyper-seasonal French-inflected small plates, excellent natural wines, and punk rock soundtrack. For something more casual, head to 40-year-old Beacon Hill standby Billiard Hoang for some of the city’s best pho and banh mi, plus a round of pool. Renee Erickson’s Sea Creatures restaurant group has come to define PNW cuisine in the past couple of decades, and her oyster bar, the Walrus and the Carpenter , is a must-visit. And you can’t forget about Communion , the soul food restaurant in the Central District from chef Kristi Brown.

Bakeries: One underrated aspect of Washington State’s agricultural prowess is the high-quality wheat that’s grown here. That local flour fuels an abundance of creative bakeries , some of which straddle the line between bakery, coffee shop, and restaurant, like Saint Bread in the University District, which was named a top bakery in the U.S. by the New York Times in 2024, and its sister cafe, the Wayland Mill . Some draw on Scandinavian baking traditions, like Queen Anne’s Byen Bakeri , while others are Asian-influenced, like the CID’s Fuji Bakery and Paper Cake Shop in Fremont, where you can get slab-style sheet-cake slices. Ben’s Bread in Phinney Ridge is a sourdough destination, and on Wednesday nights, it serves pizza that reliably and justifiably draws a massive line (you can only place an order in person).

Bars: Seattle’s bar scene is marked by countless dives , elegant cocktail lounges, and everything in between . Cocktail standouts include James Beard-semifinalist Rob Roy ; Canon , which features the nation’s largest spirits list; and Zig Zag Café , a Pike Place Market bar and restaurant where the Last Word, a famous cocktail, was reintroduced to the world by bartender Murray Stenson . And Pacific Inn , which is famous for its fish and chips , the Central District’s Twilight Exit , and Ballard institution Hattie’s Hat are some of the city’s most treasured dives. Seattle also boasts wine bars and bottle shops galore , like La Dive , a playful Capitol Hill hub for natural wine, and Le Caviste , which feels like a little slice of Paris bistro culture in Downtown Seattle.

Breweries: There’s been an exciting proliferation of breweries throughout Seattle in recent years, but Holy Mountain , with its constantly changing menu of offbeat, barrel-aged beers, is a must-visit. Cloudburst , just north of Pike Place Market, is a masterful maker of award-winning IPAs . Many breweries, too, have become hosts for Seattle’s many thriving food pop-ups , particularly Ballard’s Fair Isle Brewing . Relatively new entrant Project 9 Brewing has drawn acclaim for its wide array of beer styles, while Bizarre Brewing ’s complex, low-ABV brews have quickly become a mainstay among day-drinking beer dads.

Coffee: Seattle’s coffee shops run the gamut from lived-in hangouts that have been there for decades to trendy, new-wave espresso spots focused on lighter roasts and more diverse flavor profiles. Recently, a young generation of coffee lovers has brought renewed appreciation for Vietnamese-style phin-brewed coffee, which you can find at places like Hello Em and Phin in the International District, Coffeeholic House in Columbia City, and Fremont’s Aroom , which recently opened a second location on the city’s newly revitalized waterfront. Coffee originated in East Africa, and several spots around town are rooted in the deep-seated coffee traditions from that part of the world. You can experience an Ethiopian coffee ceremony at Lands of Origin in Pike Place Market, try specialty single-origin brews at Avole , or grab an excellent cup at one of Boon Boona ’s many locations around the city.

Views: You can’t help but notice the sparkling scenery in and around this fetching city, but some restaurants boast particularly stunning views . Ferry across Elliott Bay to dine on Hawaiian-Korean creations at Marination Ma Kai or nab an Adirondack chair on the north end of Lake Union for oysters and a skyline view at Westward .

Pike Place Market: If you’re visiting Downtown Seattle or taking a tour of the city with out-of-towners, chances are you’ll end up at Pike Place at some point . While Pike Place might have a touristy reputation, don’t let that deter you. It’s possible to take in the extravagant fish-tossing and partake in some of Seattle’s best food, whether that be the aforementioned lo-fi Filipino dining pioneer Oriental Mart or ultra-dramatic Italian American restaurant, the Pink Door , with its spinach lasagna and occasional trapeze artists.
These are the key areas of the city every self-proclaimed food lover has to survey — complete with what to eat and drink in each.

Capitol Hill is Seattle’s historically LGBTQ neighborhood and a nightlife hub. Though it’s contending with gentrification , it’s still home to many colorful queer businesses. It’s also one of Seattle’s best dining neighborhoods. See some of the finest options in our neighborhood guide . For Mexican, don’t miss Carmelo’s Tacos ; for Laotian, see Taurus Ox , which now has a burger-only spinoff restaurant, Ox Burger . A relative newcomer to the neighborhood, Ramie is making some of the most exciting and innovative moves in haute Vietnamese cuisine at the moment. If you are in the market for a high-end experience, Lark is a fine dining restaurant that is still doing it right, while LTD Edition Sushi is one of the city’s top omakase counters.

The Chinatown-International District (also known by shortened names like the CID, the International District, or the ID) is home to Chinatown, Japantown, Filipino Town, and Little Saigon, as well as too many incredible restaurants to name here. See our neighborhood dining guide for tons of options. For something more immersive, the Wing Luke Museum runs a food walking tour that is a great opportunity to learn about the rich history of the CID through the lens of its diverse cuisine. Gan Bei is a perfect late-night hangout for beer, Chinese fried chicken, and sausage clay pots, while Saigon Vietnam Deli is a great spot for a quick banh mi. The Thai restaurant E-Jae Pak Mor is famous for its dumplings with paper-thin skin . Don’t forget Tai Tung , Seattle’s oldest Chinese restaurant, founded in 1935. But for many locals, the top reason to go to the CID is the massive Asian supermarket Uwajimaya , which sells an array of products and also has plenty of hot food counters and a food court.

Once a rough-and-tumble Scandinavian fishing village, 21st-century Ballard is now startlingly hip. The neighborhood — mapped out for your dining convenience — straddles the line between modern development and the preservation of its early history. There’s plenty worth eating here, including wood-fired pizza perfectionist Delancey and Lebanese restaurant Cafe Munir . Little Beast , Eater Seattle’s 2025 restaurant of the year , takes English pub food to new heights with its meticulously sourced and prepared meats. The neighborhood also has its own brewery district with more than a dozen brewers within walking distance, including Reuben’s , Stoup , and Urban Family .

Georgetown has a history of grit and brick, but has also become a thriving culinary and cultural destination, fostering a local character that draws in visitors from all over town. You can find decadent slices of cakes at Deep Sea Sugar and Salt , wonderful vegan sandwiches at the divey Georgetown Liquor Company , top-notch handmade pasta in a romantic setting at Mezzanotte , and intricate six-course prix fixe meals at the Corson Building .

This eclectic neighborhood (see: massive troll under a bridge ), just north of Lake Union, and to the east of Ballard, harbors a fair share of standout restaurants: Chef Mutsuko Soma’s soba destination Kamonegi , the French-ish Le Coin , and Local Tide , where people line up for the succulent crab rolls, in particular. James Beard Award-winning chefs Rachel Yang and Seif Chirchi run the kitchen at Joule , known for its kalbi short ribs, local pickled vegetables, and a fresh take on Korean cuisine. If you want something sweet, check out Doce , which serves massive brioche-style doughnuts and has quickly expanded to three locations since opening in 2023 .

West Seattle’s dining scene and the picturesque Alki Beach are equally impressive. You’ll find inventive dinners using hyper-local ingredients at Driftwood , fantastic pasta in a century-old log house at Il Nido , and top-notch smoked meats at Lady Jaye , which also boasts a terrific backyard patio. Seafood fans should check out Mashiko for sushi that emphasizes sustainability; those recovering from a long night can eat breakfast (or get some hair of the dog) with a side of killer soundtrack at Easy Street Records & Cafe .
Central District , U District , Tacoma , and Seattle-Tacoma International Airport .

It’s a hot dog or sausage slathered in — wait for it — cream cheese and grilled onions. The murky origin story goes back to the late 1990s, when a bagel cart in Pioneer Square went a little rogue . Though it sounds strange, the sweet and meaty flavor combination is surprisingly satisfying (try some hot sauce on it), and even high-end restaurants will sometimes riff on the concoction for specials. You can generally find a Seattle dog at Capitol Hill stands bumping Latin dance music and selling the franks late into the night along with elotes, and at other hot dog-focused places around town .

This sticky-sweet Japanese-American dish is a Seattle specialty, popularized by Toshihiro Kasahara at Toshi’s Teriyaki Restaurant in the 1970s. You can still find Kasahara north of the city at Toshi’s Teriyaki Grill in Mill Creek; within Seattle city limits, try gluten-free options at West Seattle’s Grillbird Teriyaki .

Old-school yet relevant, Canlis is Seattle’s archetypal fine dining restaurant, which has shown a great deal of versatility over the years. In 2025, the restaurant shook up its ownership structure (now the sole owner is Mark Canlis) and suffered a much-talked-about negative review in The Seattle Times . But whoever is at the helm, Canlis remains one of the city’s most important restaurants.

This James Beard Award-winning chef channels rustic European country cooking by way of seasonal Pacific Northwest ingredients in her bright, airy, elegant spaces. She runs some of the city’s most adored spots through her Sea Creatures restaurant group, including oyster bar, the Walrus and the Carpenter, and Westward . Despite controversy over staff unionization efforts , which coincided with the closure of several restaurants in 2025, her empire continues to grow: She recently opened three new restaurants in Pioneer Square, Lowlander Brewing , Un Po Tipsy , and Mio Oh Mio . Meanwhile, her innovative Capitol Hill steakhouse Bateau, which has been closed since summer 2025, has rebranded as Jeffry’s and recently reopened with a similar menu.

A legend in his own right, this beloved chef trained with Jiro Ono (of Jiro Dreams of Sushi ) before bringing Edomae-style sushi to Seattle and defining the scene here over the past 50 years. He spent early days at Maneki and other spots around town, pioneering the use of local seafood, then two decades at namesake Shiro’s . Finally, after the world’s shortest retirement, Kashiba returned to the counter in late 2015 at Pike Place Market’s Sushi Kashiba , where you can still find him on Wednesdays and Saturdays. He’s now focused on helping the next generation of Seattle sushi chefs open their own restaurants.
